findings.name: frontend
findings.root_cause: Today's deploy set the frontend container image to nginx:1.299-alpine, which does not exist in docker.io/library/nginx (ErrImagePull NotFound), so pod frontend-b86cc5bdc-ct555 is stuck in ImagePullBackOff and the deployment has 0 ready replicas.
findings.fix: Update the Deployment's container image to a tag that exists for nginx (e.g. nginx:1.27-alpine or the intended published tag) and redeploy.

diagnosis.summary: The storefront frontend never starts because today's deploy pinned the container image to nginx:1.299-alpine, which does not exist upstream (docker.io returns NotFound). The single pod is in ImagePullBackOff/ErrImagePull, leaving the Deployment at 0/1 ready. Fix: point the Deployment at an existing nginx image tag.

findings.name: billing
findings.root_cause: Pod billing-597d6775c9-ht8g5 is stuck in Pending with CreateContainerConfigError because the container's envFrom references ConfigMap "billing-config", which does not exist in the billing namespace, so the container can never start and the Deployment never reaches Running.
findings.fix: Create the missing ConfigMap "billing-config" in namespace billing with the expected keys (or remove the envFrom reference from the billing Deployment if it is no longer needed).

diagnosis.summary: The billing Deployment's pod is stuck in Pending: kubelet reports CreateContainerConfigError 'configmap \"billing-config\" not found' (repeated 14x), and the pod spec shows envFrom referencing that ConfigMap. The only ConfigMap in the billing namespace is kube-root-ca.crt, confirming billing-config is missing. Fix: create the billing-config ConfigMap or drop the envFrom reference."

findings.name: nightly-export
findings.root_cause: Both nightly-export pods exited with code 2 because the export process could not write its output file (permission denied on /exports/orders-2026-09-27.csv), so no export was produced and the Job hit its backoff limit
findings.fix: Give the export container write access to the destination volume/mount for /exports (fix mount ownership/permissions or the target path in the Job spec), then re-run the job

diagnosis.summary: The nightly-export Job failed both attempts: each pod's export container logged 'ERROR: permission denied: cannot write /exports/orders-2026-09-27.csv' and exited with code 2, so no CSV was produced and the Job reached BackoffLimitExceeded. Root cause is a write-permission problem on the export output location; the Job spec/volume configuration must be fixed before re-running.

status namespace is healthy: deployment status-page 1/1 ready (rs-deployment-status-page), no problem pods, only Normal events (scheduled/pulled/started), and Service status-page has 1 ready endpoint on port 80 (ds-service-status-page). Ready for the demo.

findings.name: cache
findings.root_cause: cache pod is Pending/Unschedulable because its nodeSelector requires disktype=nvme, but the only node doctor-lab-control-plane has disktype=standard, so 0/1 nodes match.
findings.fix: Remove or correct the nodeSelector disktype=nvme on the cache Deployment (node is disktype=standard), or add an nvme-labeled node to the pool.

diagnosis.summary: The cache deployment's single pod cannot be scheduled: it carries nodeSelector disktype=nvme while the cluster's only node is labeled disktype=standard, producing FailedScheduling 'didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector'. Root cause is the mismatched nodeSelector in the cache Deployment spec.

findings.name: checkout
findings.root_cause: Service checkout selects app=checkout-v2, but the healthy checkout Deployment labels its pods app=checkout, so the selector matches 0 pods and has 0 ready endpoints; clients hitting the Service VIP get connection refused even though the pod itself is fine.
findings.fix: Align the labels: change the Service selector to app=checkout (or relabel the Deployment's pod template with app=checkout-v2) so it matches the running pods.

diagnosis.summary: checkout/checkout pods are healthy (1/1 ready), but the checkout Service selects app=checkout-v2 while the Deployment's pods are labeled app=checkout. The Service therefore has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints, causing connection refused on calls to the service. Fix by aligning the Service selector or the Deployment pod labels."

findings.name: report-worker
findings.root_cause: Container is OOMKilled (exit 137) within seconds of each start because its memory limit is only 32Mi, so it restarts every few seconds with no application error in the logs.
findings.fix: Raise the report-worker container memory limit (and request) above its actual working-set size, e.g. limit 128Mi / request 64Mi, then verify it stays up.

diagnosis.summary: report-worker in namespace reports crash-loops: pod shows OOMKilled exit code 137 on every start (3 restarts), BackOff events, and its log contains only 'warming report cache' — consistent with being killed by the kernel before any app error. The Deployment sets a 32Mi memory limit, which the workload exceeds almost immediately. Fix is to raise the memory limit/request in the Deployment spec; no other objects are affected.

findings.name: orders-api
findings.root_cause: orders-api crashes on startup (exit 1) because its container spec defines no env or envFrom, so DATABASE_URL is never provided; the app fatals on missing config, the pod crash-loops (5 restarts), and the Deployment has 0/1 ready replicas, taking the orders page down.
findings.fix: Add DATABASE_URL to the orders-api Deployment (env or an envFrom Secret/ConfigMap reference), then roll the pods.

diagnosis.summary: orders/orders-api is crash-looping: the container logs 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set' and exits 1 (5 restarts, BackOff). The Deployment's container spec has no env or envFrom entries, so DATABASE_URL is never injected; no ConfigMap in the namespace provides it either. With 0/1 ready replicas the orders page is down. Fix: add DATABASE_URL to the Deployment's container env (or a Secret/envFrom) and roll the pods.

findings.name: defaults
findings.root_cause: statement-builder sets no memory limit in its spec, but the namespace LimitRange 'defaults' injects a 32Mi default limit (16Mi request); the workload's statement build loads ~50MB of ledger rows into memory, exceeds 32Mi, and is OOMKilled (exit 137) in a restart loop.
findings.fix: Raise or remove the default memory limit in LimitRange finance/defaults (or set an explicit, adequate memory limit on the statement-builder container), so the ~50MB working set is not capped at 32Mi.

diagnosis.summary: statement-builder is OOMKilled (exit 137, 3 restarts) despite setting no memory limit: the finance namespace LimitRange 'defaults' applies a 32Mi default memory limit to containers without one. The job loads ~50MB of data into memory, exceeding that injected cap. Fix is in the LimitRange (or an explicit limit on the Deployment).

findings.name: ledger
findings.root_cause: ledger container panics at startup with 'invalid config key "retries": expected integer, got "three"' and exits 2, so the Deployment is crash-looping (3 restarts) and never becomes ready.
findings.fix: Correct the ledger configuration: set retries to an integer value (the current config supplies the string "three") and redeploy the ledger Deployment.

findings.name: ledger-api
findings.root_cause: Service ledger-api selects app=ledger-gateway, but no pod in the namespace carries that label (labels present are app=ledger and app=ledger-api), so it has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints and cannot answer traffic.
findings.fix: Point the Service selector at the real gateway pods, e.g. change selector app=ledger-gateway to app=ledger-api (or add the app=ledger-gateway label to the ledger-api pods).

diagnosis.summary: Two independent faults in namespace ledger. (1) The ledger Deployment crash-loops: its container logs show a startup panic 'invalid config key \"retries\": expected integer, got \"three\"', exit code 2, BackOff events; fix is correcting the config value. (2) Service ledger-api does not answer because its selector app=ledger-gateway matches no pods (ready pods are labeled app=ledger-api / app=ledger); fix is aligning the selector or pod labels."

findings.name: stock-db
findings.root_cause: stock-db's container has a 24Mi memory limit; after ~25s it runs 'loading stock index into memory' (tail /dev/zero), exceeds the limit, is OOMKilled (exit 137) and crash-loops in BackOff — so port 5432 is down and stock-api exits with 'database unavailable'.
findings.fix: Raise stock-db's memory limit (and set a matching request) above what the index load needs, e.g. 256Mi, instead of 24Mi.

diagnosis.summary: stock-api crashes because its dependency stock-db is unreachable: stock-db is OOMKilled (exit 137, 3 restarts, BackOff events) because its Deployment sets a 24Mi memory limit while the container loads an index into memory right after startup. The stock-api pod is a victim; fixing stock-db's memory limit restores connectivity.

findings.name: ml-trainer
findings.root_cause: ml-trainer requests 64 CPU ("64" cores) while the only node has 2 allocatable CPU, so the scheduler reports '1 Insufficient cpu' and preemption is not helpful; the pod stays Pending.
findings.fix: Lower the ml-trainer container CPU request to a value the node can satisfy (e.g. 1 or 2 cores instead of 64); alternatively add node capacity.

diagnosis.summary: ml-trainer pod is Pending because its Deployment requests 64 CPU on a cluster whose single node offers only 2 allocatable CPU. Scheduler events confirm 'Insufficient cpu' with preemption not helpful. The fix is to reduce the CPU request in the ml-trainer Deployment spec (or add nodes). No other workloads are affected.

findings.name: accounts-api
findings.root_cause: The wait-for-db init container loops on `nc -z accounts-db 5432`, but no Service named accounts-db exists in the namespace (the database is exposed as accounts-database), so DNS resolution fails with 'bad address' and the pod stays stuck in Init:Running.
findings.fix: Change the init container's wait command to target the existing service name, e.g. `until nc -z -w 2 accounts-database 5432; do sleep 3; done` (or create an accounts-db alias service).

diagnosis.summary: accounts-api has been Pending for ~20 minutes because its init container wait-for-db cannot resolve the hostname it waits on. The init command probes `accounts-db:5432`, but the only service in the namespace is `accounts-database` (which is healthy: 1 matching pod, 1 ready endpoint). DNS lookup of accounts-db fails ('nc: bad address'), so the init loop never exits and the main container never starts. Fix: point the init container at accounts-database (or add an accounts-db service).

findings.name: mailer
findings.root_cause: mailer pod uses dns_policy:None with nameserver 10.96.0.99 which does not resolve cluster service names, so nc smtp-relay fails with 'bad address' and the container exits with code 1 repeatedly
findings.fix: Change the mailer Deployment's dnsPolicy back to ClusterFirst (or remove the custom dnsConfig) so pods use the cluster DNS at 10.96.0.10

diagnosis.summary: The smtp-relay is NOT down — its pod is Running/Ready and the Service has 1 ready endpoint. The mailer cannot reach it because the mailer Deployment sets dnsPolicy:None with a non-functional nameserver (10.96.0.99), causing all DNS lookups to fail. Fix: restore dnsPolicy to ClusterFirst in the mailer Deployment.

findings.name: pricing-api
findings.root_cause: Clients hitting the pricing-api Service on port 80 get connection refused because the Service's targetPort is 8080, but the pricing-api container listens on containerPort 80; traffic is forwarded to a closed port even though the pod itself is healthy and ready.

diagnosis.summary: pricing-api pods are healthy and ready (1/1, no problem pods), so the connection-refused comes from the Service layer. The Service pricing-api forwards port 80 -> targetPort 8080, but the nginx-based pricing-api container declares containerPort 80 and serves there; nothing listens on 8080 in the pod, so every proxied connection is refused. Fix: set the Service targetPort to 80.

findings.fix: Raise the pods limit in ResourceQuota team-quota (e.g. to >=5) or move renderer to a namespace/quota that allows more pods.

ReplicaSet events show repeated FailedCreate 'exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=2, limited: pods=2'. No problem pods; the two existing pods are healthy. Fix: raise the pods limit on team-quota.

findings.name: thumbnailer
findings.root_cause: log-shipper buffers 4Mi batches to emptyDir /buffer because the upstream collector is unreachable, exceeding its own 20Mi ephemeral-storage limit, so kubelet evicts the whole pod every few minutes and the Deployment replaces it.

rejected_submission.summary: media/thumbnailer pods are repeatedly evicted: the log-shipper sidecar in the thumbnailer Deployment writes 4Mi log batches to an emptyDir (/buffer) because its upstream collector is unreachable, and the container's 20Mi ephemeral-storage limit is exceeded within ~15s. The node then evicts the pod ("Pod ephemeral local storage usage exceeds the total limit of containers 20Mi") and the ReplicaSet recreates it, producing the observed disappear-and-replace loop. Root cause object: Deployment media/thumbnailer (log-shipper resources + unbounded buffering).

findings.fix: Fix the liveness probe in Deployment search-web: remove the busy-loop from the exec command (just `wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/`) and/or raise timeoutSeconds above ~5s.

diagnosis.summary: search-web restarts with clean logs because its liveness probe is broken, not the app. The probe's exec command runs a 300,000-iteration shell busy-loop before the wget check, with timeoutSeconds=1 — it always times out. Nginx starts fine and exits gracefully on SIGQUIT (code 0). Fix: correct the probe command in Deployment search-web."
